title: POC capacity & burst guardrails - PraxisWorks scoping
summary: Discovery+POC scoping to define success criteria for a reserved GPU pilot with burst capacity and fallback policies. Customer cares about predictable latency for low-latency chat and batch reranking, cost controls, SOC2/compliance, and a non-disruptive failover to hosted or smaller quantized model. Agreed next steps: Redwood to share costed pilot options, benchmark plan, and security pack; customer to provide traffic profile and a short prompt set for quality checks.
topics: Reserved GPUs sizing and burst strategy
action_items: Alex Kim | Send two pilot pricing options (reserved 8xA10 + burst pool vs reserved 4xA10 + larger burst) | 2027-01-21
Samira Patel | Draft benchmark plan and measurement dashboard template | 2027-01-22
Maya Thompson | Share 2-week traffic histogram and token distribution CSV | 2027-01-21
Lena Ruiz | Request SOC 2 + encryption docs from Redwood and confirm KMS requirements | 2027-01-24
Owen Park | Provide list of top 20 prompt patterns for quality/regression checks | 2027-01-22
next_steps: Redwood to email pilot proposal + cost spreadsheet and security pack
Schedule a 60-min benchmark kick-off once traffic file is received
Run an initial 4-hour smoke benchmark (p50/p95/p99) then a 24-hour soak
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-19
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 57 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Samira (Redwood SE), Diego (Redwood CR), Jared (CTO PraxisWorks), Maya (Platform Eng), Owen (ML Infra), Lena (Security), Ben (Product)

Auto-summary (auto gen, lightly edited): Discussed POC scope: reserved GPU baseline, burst pool, automated fallbacks to hosted models, quantization options, cost vs latency trade-offs, success criteria and benchmarks.

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate the time. we scheduled an hour to nail down scope for the pilot for PraxisWorks — the reserved capacity + burst plan. quick intros?
[00:12] Jared: Jared Lin here, CTO. we want to validate cost predictability and maintain chat latency under 200 ms p95 for interactive flows, and also handle periodic batch reranks without paying through the nose.
[00:26] Maya: Maya, platform eng. I'm the one who'll coordinate the traffic profile and run the integrations.
[00:32] Owen: Owen, ml infra. curious about GPU sizing and the KV cache behavior with our short-chat use case.
[00:38] Lena: Lena from security; we'll need SOC2 artifacts and we'll want to lock down KMS and SSO.
[00:44] Ben: Ben, product — I'm here for the success criteria and timelines.
[00:49] Alex: Great. Samira, Diego — quick shots?
[00:52] Samira: Samira Patel, solutions eng. I'll walk through backlog sizing and benchmarks, and propose a pilot runbook.
[00:58] Diego: Diego Morales, customer reliability, I'll be your ops contact for rollout questions.

[02:00] Samira: To set expectations — we typically do a reserved baseline so you get predictable throughput, then a burst pool for spikes. two common patterns: reserve for steady-state QPS and let burst handle the daily peaks; or reserve smaller and accept more frequent bursting if cost is the main constraint. Which do you prefer?
[02:30] Jared: Cost is critical but so is UX. If p95 goes above, say, 200-250 ms for chat it's noticeable. so I'm leaning to reserve enough to keep latency for the top 80% flows, and then burst for the tail.
[02:45] Samira: That's common. For sizing we need your 2-week traffic histogram (QPS by minute), avg token lengths, and top prompt sizes. can you share that?
[02:58] Maya: Yes we can export that — I'll put it in the sheet. any preferred format? CSV with minute buckets?
[03:05] Samira: Minute buckets are ideal. also include the largest batch jobs schedule — like nightly rerank jobs, and any predicted campaign spikes.

[04:10] Owen: Quick technical Q — how do you handle KV cache warmup when routing between reserved and burst GPUs? we've seen cold-cache penalties earlier with other vendors.
[04:28] Diego: yeah we noticed mismatch when sessions move; cache miss causes long tail.
[04:35] Samira: Good question. Redwood runtime supports continuous KV cache and cross-node prewarming for active sessions. in the pilot we can pin session affinity to reserved pools for logged-in users to avoid warmups, and optionally prefetch top-k tokens into burst nodes for predicted spikes. there are trade-offs in memory usage.
[05:05] Owen: ok that helps. can we test cache prewarming as part of the benchmark?
[05:12] Samira: Absolutely — test matrix will include cold/warm runs.

[06:00] Ben: Success metrics — to be concrete, we want: p95 latency <= 200 ms for interactive; tail p99 under 400 ms unless fallback triggers; cost per 1k requests to be X (we'll quantify once we see your pricing); failures under 0.1% and graceful degradation to hosted.
[06:28] Alex: Perfect — we'll convert that into SLA-like success criteria in the pilot doc. any red lines?
[06:33] Lena: From security, red lines are no customer PII leaving the VPC or persistent logs beyond retention policy. we need KMS integration, audit logging, and SSO with SAML. also, can the platform support on-prem/private for final rollout?
[06:54] Samira: Yes on-prem/private is an option; for the pilot we recommend VPC-only with customer-managed KMS if you prefer. we have SOC2 docs and an enterprise pack we can share.

[07:40] Jared: Timeline — we're hoping for a 6-week pilot: week 0-1 prep and infra, week 2 short smoke benchmarks, week 3-4 soak and regressions, week 5 evaluation + handoff. is that realistic?
[08:00] Alex: Yes it's realistic if we get traffic files this week. the critical path is the data and prompt set for quality tests.
[08:08] Maya: We'll try to get the 2-week histogram and prompt set by EOD Friday.

[09:00] Samira: Benchmarks we propose: 1) 4-hour p95/p99 smoke with synthetic traffic matching your 95th percentile, 2) 24-hour soak capturing overnight batch reranks, 3) failure injection where we force a fallback to hosted model and measure end-to-end latency and error rate.
[09:30] Owen: On the fallback — what are the typical degradation patterns? do you fallback to a quantized model or to hosted Redwood?
[09:41] Samira: We support both: a lightweight quantized variant on the same pod, or a remote hosted variant. recommended pattern: first fallback to a compatible quantized local variant (lower cost, similar latency), then to hosted as a last resort. that gives predictable cost and controlled quality degradation.
[10:05] Jared: How do you route rules work? can we set percent-based fallbacks or load-based?
[10:12] Samira: You can have policy-based routing: by latency thresholds, queue depth, cost budget, model-quality guardrails, or manual canary. Also tie it to tenant-level RBAC so different teams get different policies.

[11:00] Ben: For rerank workloads, we do large batched scoring — could be thousands of candidate rows in a job. how does the reserved pool handle batching vs latency-sensitive small requests?
[11:20] Samira: The runtime supports workload-aware batching with priority lanes: low-latency lane for interactive, batch lane for large scoring jobs. the scheduler will keep tokens from batch jobs in a separate queue and use available GPU cycles when latency SLOs allow. for the pilot we recommend dedicating a fraction of reserved capacity to batch tasks or using dedicated reserved nodes for batch.
[11:52] Maya: That seems important. we have a big nightly rerank at 03:00 UTC with a 2-hour window. we'd rather not use burst for that if it blows budget.
[12:05] Samira: Then reserve for some of the batch capacity or schedule it in lower-cost windows; we can also shard the rerank across multiple nodes to avoid big spikes. we'll model cost in the pilot options.

[13:00] Lena: Security again — audit logs retention: can we control retention windows and export logs to our SIEM?
[13:12] Diego: We do forward logs; customers can configure retention and export to S3 or direct to SIEM via secure channel.
[13:22] Lena: KMS — we need CMEK supported and key rotation policies.
[13:28] Samira: Supported — Redwood supports customer-managed encryption keys and HSM integration in Private deployments; for VPC pilot we can provide CMEK with KMS.

[14:10] Jared: Pricing options — show us an actual cost delta between reserving more vs relying on burst. we want a spreadsheet.
[14:19] Alex: We'll send two costed options: option A: reserve for 80% steady-state (estimate based on your histogram), small burst buffer; option B: reserve for 50% and rely on a larger burst pool — cheaper baseline but higher burst spend. we'll include modeled p95 latency per option in the sheet.

[15:00] Ben: Benchmarks — what metrics will you capture and how will we view them?
[15:08] Samira: We'll capture p50/p95/p99, token throughput, GPU utilization, queue depths, cache hit rates, and cost per 1k tokens. dashboard will be a shared Redwood Console view with short-lived access tokens for your team.
[15:28] Diego: Can we get traces for slow requests?
[15:32] Samira: Yes, tracing hooks and request-level logs are available; we'll redact PII or mask tokens per policy.

[16:10] Owen: About quantization — you mentioned quality regressions. what's the recommended eval approach?
[16:20] Samira: We'll run the prompt set through both the float model and the quantized variants and compute a small set of metrics: pass@k (for ranking tasks), semantic-similarity scores, and an annotation sample for humans. we'll flag any regressions beyond a chosen threshold and roll out a canary.

[17:00] Jared: If the quantized variant causes subtle regressions in product-critical flows (billing language, safety), what's the rollback behavior?
[17:12] Samira: Automatic rollback policy is supported: if quality metrics cross a threshold we'll revert to the previous model and route new requests to hosted fallback while we investigate. can configure notifications to your team.

[18:00] Maya: Integration complexity — what SDKs and auth methods do you support?
[18:08] Alex: REST, internal SDKs, and gRPC for high-throughput. Auth via API keys or SAML OIDC for tenant access. we also support IP allowlists.
[18:23] Maya: Ok. we'll prefer SAML SSO and keys for CI jobs.

[19:00] Ben: Can we also run a short head-to-head against CloudX AI to compare p95 and cost?
[19:08] Samira: Yes, we can include a competitor baseline as an optional benchmark if you provide the test harness. we'll need to match sequence lengths and batch patterns.

[20:00] Jared: Let's talk concrete numbers — assume our steady-state is 35 QPS with spikes to 220 QPS during marketing events; average token per request 150, peak up to 600 (for long search re-rank). what does that map to in GPUs?
[20:25] Samira: Rough thumb rule — for short-chat at 150 tokens per request on a modern A10-like instance, 1 GPU can handle ~60-80 interactive qps with p95 under 200ms depending on model. for your 35 steady QPS you'd be safe reserving 1 GPU for interactive lanes; burst pool should cover the 220 spikes — maybe a 2-4 GPU burst pool depending on expected concurrency and batch overlap. but this is very rough — we'll do detailed sizing after seeing the token distrib.
[21:05] Owen: So for the pilot we'd look at reserving either 1 GPU baseline + 3 GPU burst OR reserving 2 GPUs + 1 GPU burst?
[21:15] Samira: Exactly. Option A: reserve 2 GPU baseline (lower tail latency, higher base cost) + 1 GPU burst. Option B: reserve 1 GPU baseline + 3 GPU burst (cheaper steady, more burst spend). we'll model both.

[22:00] Alex: Can we build an automated guardrail: if burst spend exceeds X% of monthly budget, throttle non-critical batch jobs and notify ops?
[22:10] Samira: Yes — Redwood has cost-aware policies that can throttle batch queues, move them to off-peak windows, or switch them to a lower-cost quantized model. we'll include policy templates in the pilot.

[23:30] Lena: Data residency — some customer data must remain in EU. do you have multi-region controls?
[23:38] Samira: Yes region pinning and routing policies let you keep traffic in a specified region. for the pilot, we can pin test workloads to a single region matching your compliance needs.

[24:40] Ben: Failure modes — if a reserved GPU pool loses nodes (maintenance), what happens to in-flight sessions?
[24:48] Diego: we shift sessions with session affinity preserved when possible; if not possible we fallback to hosted with a short token loss window. the runtime tries to minimize duplicate requests and supports graceful reconnect.

[26:00] Jared: Ok, let's capture the explicit success criteria so there's no ambiguity.
[26:08] Ben: Proposed success criteria —
 - p95 latency for interactive flows <= 200 ms for 95% of test window
 - p99 latency <= 400 ms except during forced fallback tests
 - batch rerank throughput meets job SLAs (throughput numbers TBD)
 - cost per 1k requests within agreed band compared to option baseline
 - <0.1% error rate and fallback to hosted only when policy triggers
 - no PII leakage and KMS/CMEK enabled
[27:00] Alex: We'll put these in the pilot doc as pass/fail checks.

[28:00] Samira: Now the benchmark plan details: we will run three phases — smoke, soak, and resilience. smoke is 4 hours — synthetic load matching your 95th percentile. soak is 24 hours with real-ish traffic sampling. resilience tests include node failures, cache cold starts, and fallback triggers. we'll record traces and compute p50/p95/p99 and cost.
[28:40] Maya: For soak, can we include a real user-sampled dataset?
[28:46] Samira: Yes, sanitized/hashed samples are fine. we'll sign an NDA addendum if needed.

[30:00] Owen: For the resilience tests, how much of an artificial spike will you simulate?
[30:10] Samira: We'll simulate 3x your 95th percentile for short windows and sustained 1.5x for 30 mins. we can adjust thresholds.

[31:00] Jared: About instrumentation — will we get raw GPU metrics?
[31:06] Samira: GPU utilization, memory, queue depth, and KV cache hit rates will be in the console. we can also provide periodic CSV exports.

[32:00] Ben: On black-box concerns from procurement — cost amortization, invoice structure, SLAs. can you do month-to-month or minimum commit?
[32:12] Alex: For pilots we typically do month-to-month with a small reserved commit. for Dedicated/Private we offer annual reserved contracts. we'll put the pilot terms in the proposal.

[33:00] Maya: How do rollouts look post-pilot? if the pilot hits success we want a smooth move to dedicated reserved pool without switching APIs.
[33:12] Samira: Exactly — same API. we can pin model versions and migrate capacity transparently. the Console supports rollouts and canary traffic splits.

[34:00] Lena: Security quick checklist we need in the doc: SOC2 report, pen test summary, data encryption, KMS options, SSO/SAML config guide, audit log export, RBAC controls.
[34:20] Samira: We'll attach the enterprise security pack with all those docs.

[35:30] Ben: Let's capture the pilot milestones and dates —
 - Receive traffic + prompts: by 2027-01-21 (customer)
 - Redwood sends pilot proposal + cost spreadsheet: by 2027-01-21
 - Kickoff benchmark: 2027-01-25
 - Smoke run: 2027-01-26
 - 24-hour soak: 2027-01-28
 - Evaluation & decision: 2027-02-02
[35:56] Alex: That timeline looks feasible assuming files come on time.

[36:30] Owen: A small note on tracing: we'd like to tag traces with tenant IDs and request types so we can filter interactive vs batch.
[36:40] Samira: yes tag support exists; we'll share recommended tagging keys.

[37:30] Jared: Are there any pitfalls you've seen with similar pilots?
[37:36] Samira: Typical pitfalls: 1) not providing representative traffic (over-optimistic), 2) not isolating batch vs interactive lanes causing latency interference, 3) missing prompt edge-cases for quantized models. we will help avoid those by a detailed test matrix.

[38:50] Ben: For regulatory reasons we may need audit logs for 7 years in one line of business — is long-term archiving supported?
[38:58] Samira: We support export to your S3 with lifecycle rules; long-term retention is doable with enterprise add-on.

[40:00] Maya: Anything about model upgrades during pilot? we might want to test a model patch.
[40:08] Samira: We'll do canary model rollouts and a rollback window in the runbook. automated regression alerts will fire if semantic similarity drops beyond threshold.

[41:00] Alex: Let's step through the costing assumptions quickly so you can prep procurement — baseline reserved price, burst per-minute billing, data egress assumptions, and support fees.
[41:12] Samira: We'll put a cost tab with baseline assumptions: GPU type (A10-like), reserved hourly, burst per-minute for on-demand nodes, storage costs for KV caches, and observability add-ons.

[42:00] Jared: Ok, security — one more: do you support BYOK and HSM?
[42:06] Samira: Yes, BYOK and HSM support in Private deployments; for VPC pilot we can do CMEK backed by your KMS.

[43:00] Ben: Competitors — we looked at CloudX AI and Infera. What differentiates Redwood for us?
[43:08] Alex: We emphasize production predictability and unified control plane across hosted/dedicated/private. smaller vendors sometimes force either all-hosted or self-managed; Redwood tries to provide the same API and rollout tools across modes.

[44:00] Maya: Quick check — what logs are redacted by default? tokens? PII?
[44:08] Samira: By default we redact token content and sensitive fields; we can configure masking rules.

[45:00] Jared: Are there limits on request size or token limits?
[45:06] Samira: We support up to a model-defined max; for large scoring jobs we suggest streaming APIs and batching. we'll document exact limits per model in the pilot doc.

[46:00] Diego: Ops question — who will be our escalation contact during pilot runs?
[46:06] Alex: We'll assign a primary AE and an on-call SE. Diego, you'll get a Slack channel and pager rotation as needed.

[47:00] Ben: Any legal procurement flags?
[47:06] Alex: Standard pilot MSA, data addendum and SOC2 NDA; we'll coordinate with your procurement.

[48:00] Samira: Wrapping up the benchmark plan again: smoke generates p50/p95/p99, soak adds longer horizon and batch overlap, resilience runs failure injections and fallback sequences. we'll produce consolidated report with charts and CSVs.

[49:00] Maya: We'll be ready to get the files Friday.

[50:00] Jared: Last quick thing — can we test disaster fallback to a hot-backup region?
[50:08] Samira: Yes, cross-region replicas and fallback routing are supported for critical flows; for pilot we can include a single cross-region failover test.

[51:00] Lena: I'll look over the security pack and respond with redlines. expect a few questions on key rotation windows.

[52:00] Alex: Great. To recap — Redwood sends pilot proposal + cost model + security pack; PraxisWorks sends traffic histograms and prompt set; schedule kickoff for Jan 25th. Samira will own the bench plan; Alex will own commercial.

[53:00] Ben: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.

[53:30] End notes: shared artifacts: link: https://redwood.app/pilot-proposal/PWX-2027 (placeholder), security pack link: https://redwood.app/security/enterprise-pack (placeholder), benchmark-template: https://redwood.app/benchmarks/template.csv (placeholder).

[54:10] Alex: I'll follow up with the email and attach the proposal. Thanks all.

Caveats in transcript: occasional mis-attributions and auto-caption errors present; some jargon spelled inconsistently (A10 vs A100 mention in one note).
